title: Pronouns and respect
description: Choose the right word for 'you' and 'he/she' - polite, familiar or intimate - and match the verb ending to it.

guide.title: Three words for 'you'
guide.text:
Bengali makes you choose a level of respect every time you say 'you'.

আপনি (aapni) - polite. For strangers, older people, teachers, officials, your friends' parents, anyone you would call Mr or Ms. When in doubt, use this.

তুমি (tumi) - familiar. For friends, colleagues of your own age, your spouse, children, and usually your own parents and relatives. Moving from আপনি to তুমি is a step of friendship, and the older or senior person normally suggests it.

তুই (tui) - intimate. For close childhood friends, younger brothers and sisters, small children, and by some people to servants or in anger. Used to the wrong person it is insulting. Learn to recognise it; do not use it until a Bengali friend uses it with you.

The plurals are আপনারা (aapnaaraa), তোমরা (tomraa) and তোরা (toraa).

guide.title: The verb ending follows the pronoun
guide.text:
Each level has its own verb ending, and the same five endings run through every tense. In the simple present of করা (to do) they are:

আমি করি - I do (-i)
তুমি করো - you do, familiar (-o)
তুই করিস - you do, intimate (-ish)
সে করে - he/she does, ordinary (-e)
আপনি করেন, তিনি করেন - you do (polite), he/she does (respected) (-en)

Notice that polite 'you' and respected 'he/she' share one ending. The verb is the same for singular and plural: আমরা করি 'we do', তারা করে 'they do'.

Because the ending tells you the level, mixing them - আপনি with a তুমি ending - is a real mistake, like saying 'you is' in English, and it can sound rude.

guide.title: He and she: one word, two levels, three distances
guide.text:
There is no difference between 'he' and 'she'. Instead Bengali marks respect and distance.

Ordinary (for friends, children, people you would call তুমি or তুই, and in neutral narration): সে (she) 'he/she' in general; ও (o) 'he/she over there'; এ (e) 'he/she right here'.

Respected (for anyone you would call আপনি, and for elders): তিনি (tini); উনি (uni) 'that person there'; ইনি (ini) 'this person here'. These take the -en ending.

In everyday speech ও and উনি are the commonest; সে and তিনি are used for someone not present and in writing.

Plurals: তারা (taaraa), ওরা (oraa), এরা (eraa) 'they'; respected তাঁরা (taanraa), ওঁরা (onraa), এঁরা (enraa) - spelt with the nasal sign. 'It' for a thing is সেটা, ওটা or এটা.

guide.title: The full set
guide.text:
I: আমি (aami) - we: আমরা (aamraa)
you, polite: আপনি - আপনারা
you, familiar: তুমি - তোমরা
you, intimate: তুই - তোরা
he/she, ordinary: সে, ও, এ - তারা, ওরা, এরা
he/she, respected: তিনি, উনি, ইনি - তাঁরা, ওঁরা, এঁরা

As the object of a verb ('me', 'you', 'him/her') the pronouns take the ending -কে: আমাকে (aamaake), আপনাকে (aapnaake), তোমাকে (tomaake), তোকে (toke), তাকে (taake), ওকে (oke), তাঁকে (taanke), ওঁকে (onke). The possessive forms ('my', 'your') are in the next unit.
